Duplicate Purchase Events After Adding the Conversions API
The Meta pixel and Conversions API should deduplicate to one event. When they do not, you double-count revenue or lose half of it. How to prove yours works.

Running the Meta pixel and Conversions API together should deduplicate to one event. When it does not, you either double-count revenue or silently lose half of it. How deduplication actually works and how to prove yours is functioning.
Paid Ads & Conversion Tracking Specialist
CAPI duplicate purchase events
Why am I seeing duplicate purchase events after installing the Conversions API?

Because the browser pixel and the server are both sending the purchase, and Meta cannot tell they are the same event. Deduplication requires both sides to send a matching event_id, and ideally the same event_name. If the IDs differ, Meta counts two separate purchases.
What is event_id used for in the Meta Conversions API?

It is the deduplication key. When the pixel and the Conversions API both send an event with the same event_name and the same event_id within Meta deduplication window, Meta keeps one and discards the other.
Is it bad to run the Meta pixel and Conversions API at the same time?

No, running both is the recommended setup because the server side captures conversions the browser misses. It is only a problem when deduplication is misconfigured, in which case you either double-count or lose events.

You installed CAPI and your revenue doubled. It didn’t.
<t0>Kamran Arshad</t0><t1>12 Aug 2026</t1><t2>8 min read</t2>

Duplicate purchases after a Conversions API install almost always mean one thing: <t0>the browser and the server are sending different <t1>event_id</t1> values</t0> for the same purchase. Meta deduplicates on matching <t2>event_name</t2> plus <t3>event_id</t3>. If the IDs differ, it has no way to know the two events are the same order, so it counts both.
The dangerous version is the opposite failure, where IDs collide and you silently lose real sales.

Installing the Conversions API is the right decision. Browser tracking loses events to ad blockers, tracking prevention, broken sessions and abandoned page loads, and a server-side feed recovers a good share of them. Almost everyone should be running both.

But “running both” means Meta now receives two reports of every purchase, and the only thing stopping it counting each one twice is a shared identifier. Get that identifier wrong in one direction and your revenue doubles on paper. Get it wrong in the other and your revenue quietly halves.
How deduplication actually works
Meta matches on two fields together: <t0>event_name</t0> and <t1>event_id</t1>. Both must agree.
✗ Counted twice
✓ Deduplicated to one

The rule is simple to state and easy to break in practice, because the two sides are usually built by different systems at different times. The browser event is generated by a theme or a tag manager; the server event is generated by an app, a middleware service, or your own code. Nothing forces them to agree, and nothing warns you when they do not.
Choosing an identifier that cannot drift
The identifier must be <t0>unique per order</t0> and <t1>identical across both paths</t1>. Those two requirements rule out most of what people reach for first.

Timestamps are the worst offender and the most tempting, because they look unique. They are not: two orders in the same second collide, and the browser’s clock is not your server’s clock. A UUID is fine <t0>only</t0> if it is generated once and then passed to the other side, if each side generates its own, you have built a duplication machine.
<t0>The subtler failure: silent loss</t0>

Everyone worries about double-counting because it is visible. The worse bug is an identifier that is not unique, a checkout ID reused across orders, or a value that repeats. Then Meta correctly deduplicates two <t0>genuinely different</t0> purchases into one, and you lose real revenue from your reporting with no error anywhere.
Double-counting looks like good news and gets investigated. Silent loss looks like a slow decline and gets blamed on the ads.
Proving it works: not assuming it does
Configured is not the same as working. Here is the test that settles it, and it takes about fifteen minutes.
<t0>Place one real order</t0>A real purchase through the real checkout, not a test link. Note the order number.
<t0>Capture the browser event ID</t0>Open DevTools before checking out, filter the Network tab for <t1>facebook</t1>, complete the order, and read the <t2>eventID</t2> on the Purchase request.
<t0>Capture the server event ID</t0>From your CAPI integration’s logs, or from Events Manager, find the server-side event for that same order and read its <t1>event_id</t1>.
<t0>Compare them character for character</t0>Not similar. Identical. A prefix on one side (<t1>order_1047</t1> versus <t2>1047</t2>) is a failure, not a detail.

<t0>Check the deduplication reporting</t0>In Events Manager, open the Purchase event and look at how it is being received. A correctly deduplicated setup shows both browser and server as sources for the same event, not two separate event totals.
<t0>Reconcile a full week</t0>Compare your store’s order count with Events Manager purchases for a settled week. Meaningfully above your order count means duplication. Meaningfully below means loss.
The number that tells you it is working

Once deduplication is right, the metric worth watching is <t0>Event Match Quality</t0>. It reflects how much identifying information you send with each event, hashed email, phone, name, location, click identifiers, and it drives how well Meta can attribute a conversion to the person who saw the ad.

This is where the Conversions API earns its keep. Your server knows the customer’s email and phone number because they just bought something. The browser often does not. Sending that data server-side, correctly hashed, is usually a bigger win than recovering the blocked events in the first place.
<t0>Hash it, and check that you did</t0>

Customer identifiers must be SHA-256 hashed before they are sent. This is not a performance nicety, it is the difference between sending Meta a hash and sending Meta your customers’ raw personal data. If you are building the integration yourself, verify the hashing on a real payload before you go live, because a bug here is a data protection incident rather than a tracking bug.
What I am not claiming

I have not given you a target Event Match Quality score or an expected uplift from installing CAPI. Both depend entirely on what customer data you can legitimately collect, your checkout, and your traffic, and every benchmark I have seen published comes from a vendor whose product improves the number they are benchmarking.
Measure your own baseline before the change, measure again after it has run for a full attribution window, and compare against yourself. That comparison is worth more than anyone’s published average.

A Google Ads account audit for lead generation: six checks, in order
<t0>Kamran Arshad</t0><t1>10 Oct 2026</t1><t2>3 min read</t2>

A useful Google Ads audit for a business that lives on phone calls and enquiry forms checks six things in order: advertiser verification, Search and Display separation, location targeting, negative keywords, conversion tracking for forms and calls, and ad group structure by service.
I ran this sequence on a dental clinic's account that had never been properly configured.

Most Google Ads audit checklists start with bids and ad copy. For a lead-generation business I start further upstream, because bids and copy cannot repair an account that shows ads in the wrong place, to the wrong searches, with no record of what happened next.
The six checks
Advertiser verification

Google can require advertiser identity verification. On the clinic's account it had not been completed, which put campaign delivery at risk. Look for a verification notice first, because nothing else matters if ads stop serving.
Search and Display kept apart

The clinic's campaigns mixed the Search and Display Networks. Display was using budget without producing enquiries, so I separated the two and paused Display. Check the network settings of every campaign.
Location targeting
The campaigns targeted the whole world instead of Islamabad, where the clinic operates. Open each campaign's location settings and confirm the places listed are the places you serve.
Negative keywords
There were no negative keywords, so a share of the budget went to searches with no local intent. Read the search terms report for the last 30 days and add what should never have triggered an ad.
Conversion tracking for forms and calls

Neither form submissions nor phone calls were tracked, so every decision rested on clicks alone. I set up Google Tag Manager triggers for form submissions and click-to-call taps and linked those events to Google Ads.
Ad groups by service
I researched local search terms and grouped keywords by service, such as teeth cleaning, implants and whitening, so each ad can match what the person typed.
What changed on the clinic's account

After the rebuild the account was Search-only, targeted to Islamabad, with a negative keyword list and tracking in place. For the first time the clinic could see which ads, keywords and campaigns produced real patient enquiries.

One dental clinic account in Islamabad. It is one account, not a study, and it is not a UK, US, Canadian or Australian account. The six checks apply to any lead-generation account because they sit upstream of bidding, but the specific problems I found are this clinic's.

It does not cover bidding strategy, ad copy or landing pages. Those matter, and they work better once the six upstream checks pass, because only then can you trust the data they rely on.

Google Ads Call Tracking for Local Service Businesses
Most tracking guides assume an online store. If your conversion is a phone call, the failures differ. Four ways to track Google Ads calls, and where each fails.

Almost every conversion tracking guide is written for online stores. If your conversion is a phone call, the failure modes are completely different. Here are the four ways to track calls from Google Ads, what each one actually measures, and where they go wrong.
Google Ads call tracking
How do I track phone calls from Google Ads?

There are four methods: call extensions using a Google forwarding number, calls from a website using a dynamic number swap, static click-to-call tracking, and a third-party call tracking platform. Each measures something slightly different, and only some of them attribute the call back to a specific keyword.
Does Google Ads call tracking record calls?

Google Ads can record calls made through Google forwarding numbers where the feature is available, and this is subject to local law and disclosure requirements. Tracking that a call happened and recording its contents are separate decisions with separate legal obligations.
Why does Google Ads show calls but my phone did not ring?

A common cause is counting click-to-call taps as calls. A tap on a phone link is an intent to call, not a completed call. If you track taps rather than connected calls of a minimum duration, your reported conversions will exceed the calls you actually received.

Google Ads call tracking, for businesses whose customers ring instead of buy
<t0>Kamran Arshad</t0><t1>12 Aug 2026</t1><t2>9 min read</t2>

If your conversion is a phone call rather than a checkout, almost every tracking guide online is written for someone else. There are four ways to track calls from Google Ads: <t0>call extensions, dynamic number insertion on your website, static click-to-call, and a third-party platform</t0>, and they measure different things.
The most common mistake is counting a tap on a phone link as a call. It is not one. It is an intention.

Read any article about conversion tracking and you will find yourself in an ecommerce store. Purchase events, cart values, return on ad spend. That is not much use if you are a dentist, a carpet cleaner, a plumber or a physiotherapist, where the money arrives because someone picked up a phone.
The failure modes are genuinely different, and they are worse, because a phone call leaves no trace in your website analytics at all unless you deliberately make it leave one.

Why counting taps quietly destroys your bidding

A tap on a <t0>tel:</t0> link means someone was interested enough to open their dialler. It does not mean they pressed the green button. It does not mean you answered. It does not mean the call lasted longer than four seconds before they realised you were closed.

If you feed taps into Google Ads as conversions, Smart Bidding optimises toward <t0>people who tap</t0>. Those are not the same people as <t1>customers who book</t1>. The gap between the two is where your budget goes.

✓ What you should count

The single highest-leverage change most local advertisers can make is applying a <t0>minimum call duration</t0> before a call counts as a conversion. Sixty seconds is a sensible starting point for most service businesses: long enough to exclude wrong numbers and immediate hang-ups, short enough to include a quick “can you come Tuesday?”

The second was <t0>Mr Expert Carpet Cleaning</t0> in Slough, where the site was rebuilt from scratch with tracking designed in rather than bolted on, including a server-side GTM container. That one taught me the lesson in the next section.
The failure nobody warns you about: the form that emails

Most local service sites use a contact form that composes an email and sends it. If that send fails, a bad SMTP configuration, a spam filter, a full inbox, the lead does not go to a queue for retry. It ceases to exist. There is no record that anyone ever filled the form in.

You cannot track what was never saved. So before any conversion tracking work on a local service site, I check one thing: <t0>does the form write the lead to a database before it tries to email anyone?</t0> If the answer is no, tracking is the second problem.
